title: Infinitives of purpose and purpose clauses
objectives: Use so that with its own subject and verb.
Form a negative purpose with in order not to or so as not to.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: We can explain the purpose of an action by saying why someone does it. A common way is to use to plus a base verb: ‘I went to the shop to buy milk’. Buying milk was my purpose. The infinitive follows the action and gives the reason for doing it, rather than simply adding another event.

We can also use in order to or so as to before a base verb: ‘She left early in order to catch the train’. These expressions can make the purpose explicit and are often useful in careful or formal writing. In many everyday sentences, a simple to-infinitive is natural.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: Use to, in order to or so as to followed by the base form: ‘We opened the window to get some air’. For a negative purpose, use in order not to or so as not to: ‘He spoke quietly so as not to wake the baby’. These patterns normally describe the purpose of the subject of the main clause.

A purpose clause with so that has a subject and a verb: ‘I wrote the address down so that I could remember it’. The subject after so that can be different: ‘She spoke slowly so that everyone could understand’. Modal verbs such as can, could, will or would often appear in these clauses, according to the time and meaning.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: Compare ‘I opened the window to get some air’ with ‘I opened the window so that the room could get some air’. In the first, the infinitive gives my purpose without a new subject. In the second, so that introduces a clause with its own subject, the room. Choose a clear sentence so the reader can identify the intended purpose.

For can introduce a noun describing a purpose: ‘I went to the shop for milk’. Do not confuse that with a purpose infinitive: ‘I went to the shop to buy milk’. The word for also appears in other structures, such as ‘a tool for cutting paper’; these are not the same as saying ‘for buy milk’.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: In a basic purpose sentence, do not use for directly before a base verb: say ‘I went out to buy bread’, not ‘I went out for buy bread’. Use so that with a subject and a verb: ‘She spoke slowly so that we could understand’, not ‘so that understand’.

A to-infinitive can have roles other than purpose. ‘I decided to leave’ gives the complement of decide; ‘I left to catch the bus’ expresses the purpose of leaving. Context determines the meaning. Be careful when rewriting: changing the subject or the possibility expressed by a modal can change the meaning.

examples.sentence: I went to the shop to buy milk.
examples.note: To buy introduces the purpose of going.

examples.sentence: She left early in order to catch the train.
examples.note: In order to makes the purpose explicit.

examples.sentence: He spoke quietly so as not to wake the baby.
examples.note: So as not to introduces a negative purpose.

examples.sentence: I wrote it down so that I could remember it.
examples.note: So that introduces a clause with a subject and verb.

examples.sentence: She spoke slowly so that everyone could understand.
examples.note: The purpose clause has a different subject.

examples.sentence: I went to the shop for milk.
I went to the shop to buy milk.
examples.note: To introduces the base verb buy.

examples.sentence: We saved money to buy a computer.
examples.note: The infinitive expresses the purpose of saving.

common_errors.incorrect: I went out for buy bread.
common_errors.correct: I went out to buy bread.
common_errors.reason: Use to before the base verb for this purpose.

common_errors.incorrect: She left early to catches the train.
common_errors.correct: She left early to catch the train.
common_errors.reason: Use the base form after to.

common_errors.incorrect: He spoke slowly so that understand.
common_errors.correct: He spoke slowly so that we could understand.
common_errors.reason: A so that clause needs a subject and a finite verb.

summary: Use to plus a base verb to express purpose.
Use in order not to or so as not to for a negative purpose.
Use so that plus a subject and verb for a purpose clause.
